messages.52e516dd5a100df9: A 4/4 bar has four quarter beats. A note can ring across counts without another attack; a rest requires silence while counting. Gently touch the sounding string to stop it without striking the body or pressing it to a fret. Tempo is the speed of the beat. BPM means beats per minute; in these 4/4 tasks, each beat is a quarter note. If you use an available external metronome, let one click match each spoken number: 1, 2, 3, 4. At 60 BPM, clicks are one second apart; this is an example, not a required playing speed. Choose a pace at which you can prepare the next action without rushing.
messages.35e7e36a2d025be2: On E play open, fret 1, open, fret 3 with a pause between attempts. Then A open/fret 2, then D open/fret 2. Speak string/fret and sounding name. Mute the previous note before switching. Then isolate a fretted ending: on string 3 fret 2, pluck B1 on count 1, let it ring through 2, stop on 3 and count 3–4 in silence. Ease the fretting pressure while keeping light finger contact on the string; gentle contact from a plucking finger can also stop it. Keep the other strings quiet. The intended sequence is B1 then silence, with no open A between them. Repeat on string 2 fret 2, E2 then silence, only after the first ending is clear.
messages.7324997aef8f187b: If reaching 3 strains, isolate open/1 first or shift rather than stretch. If pitch seems uncertain, separate fretting placement from external tuning; the app does not judge either. If an open A or D appears as you stop the fretted note, repeat just that ending without a pulse: stop the string with a gentle plucking-hand touch, release fretting pressure while retaining light contact, then move away only after the string is quiet. Avoid pulling the string sideways. Return to the counted B1-to-silence bar and compare the same ending.
messages.4f37f8d8a67da9f6: Choose and write a comfortable tempo. Isolate bars 3–4 root/fifth changes, then 5–6 eighths, then 7 octave crossing. At bar 8 stop on beat 3 and count through 4. Practise pairs with one silent count-in bar; connect only after reading the events. If you use an available external metronome for the comparison, write its setting as “quarter note = ___ BPM” and keep that setting for both full attempts. Count 1 2 3 4 with its four clicks before starting; place each “and” halfway between clicks, without doubling the click setting for eighth notes. If you change the tempo, begin a new pair of attempts at that setting. The click supplies a reference; it does not judge your playing.
messages.f337d688fa8aa86f: Black keys repeat in groups of two and three. C is the white key immediately left of a pair. Moving right raises pitch; moving left lowers it. White keys repeat C D E F G A B (Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Si). Neighbouring black or white keys are one semitone apart. A sharp (♯) raises a named note by one semitone; a flat (♭) lowers it. The black key between C and D can be called C♯ or D♭: two names for the same piano key. E–F and B–C have no black key between them; sharps and flats can also name white keys. These written studies use natural white-key notes.
messages.198073a51153e5ec: Find two C keys within C3–G4; an optional third C only if your keyboard has it. Name C through B in one octave, then reverse. Find a C and the D immediately to its right. Point to the black key between them: say “C sharp” and “D flat”, and check that both names point to that one key. Use relative names here; lesson 3 establishes the octave register.
messages.b4683b73a429bb93: Both hands: thumb 1, index 2, middle 3, ring 4, little 5. Let fingers curve naturally; wrists stay mobile, not locked. Press then release one key; avoid forcing a fixed hand shape. Before playing C4, use the keyboard diagram below. On an 88-key piano, middle C is the fourth C from the left (white key number 24, overall key number 40); the first key is A0. On shorter keyboards, consult the manufacturer’s key map for middle C / MIDI note 60. Manufacturers may label this C3, C4 or C5. Do not choose a C only because it looks central. If the map is unavailable, register identification is uncertain: practise relative note direction without calling a key C4 or claiming the required range. On an electronic keyboard, use its manual to check that transpose and octave-shift settings are zero before comparing sounding pitches with these labels. If you cannot confirm the settings, mark the sounding register uncertain and continue only the relative-key tasks.
messages.fa05321572c9d296: In 4/4 count 1 2 3 4. A quarter note lasts one beat, half note two, whole note four. A rest is counted silence, not an extra pause. Tempo is beats per minute; choose a comfortable slow pulse, not a pass threshold. The upper 4 means four beats in each bar; the lower 4 makes the quarter note the counting unit. A bar line starts the next group at 1 without adding silence.
messages.7205dd528c86813f: Clap on beats 1, 2, 3, 4. Then clap on 1, count and wait on 2; clap on 3, count and wait on 4. A clap is a brief onset, not a sound you hold. Next clap on 1, stay silent on 2, clap 3 and 4. After locating middle C in lesson 3, play C4 on 1 and keep its key down while counting 2; release and play on 3, hold through 4. These are two actual half notes. Repeat twice. Before each new attempt, count one silent 1 2 3 4 to prepare. While linking bars, go straight from 4 to the next 1 without another preparation bar. Let the final held note last its full counted duration before releasing.
messages.26c840b0ae3e180d: Legato connects notes with controlled release; do not keep every key down. A slur groups a phrase; a tie joins the same pitch across durations. p is soft, f loud, crescendo gradually louder. Keep volume comfortable, no forced impact. For electronic keyboards, touch response must be available and enabled for your touch to change loudness. Keep the master volume comfortable and fixed during the comparison. If two comfortable touches give the same loudness, check the manual rather than striking harder; fixed-velocity settings or a keyboard without touch response can prevent this task from producing a contrast.
messages.fa85424fbab93bdc: If keys overlap into a blur, practise two notes and release the first as the next starts. Pedal stays off. If your keyboard cannot vary loudness with touch, practise the note connections at one comfortable volume and record “dynamic contrast not assessed on this keyboard.” That device limitation is not evidence of a playing mistake.
messages.1e5299382f410392: Pitch means how high or low a tone sounds; volume means how loud it is. A nearby higher tone need not be louder. This course first uses relative directions, not fixed semitone intervals or accuracy scores. Work within a small, easy part of your voice; avoid testing your range limits.
messages.677967f6df093670: The study uses eight equal half-beat cells per 4/4 bar. Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”: each number is a beat and each “and” is halfway to the next number. V starts the stated tone/syllable; = adds no new start and continues current sound or silence; R releases sound and counts silence. = never means hold your breath. Normal breathing is allowed during rests and whenever needed. Written durations are suggestions, not physiological targets. H remains the higher-tone label; it is never the continuation symbol.
messages.d6254c4d29708317: First tap four even beats without singing; then count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” with eight evenly spaced taps. On the study, tap only each printed V while the half-beat count continues through = and R. Inspect the full silent bars 6 and 8 and the silent endings of bars 1–4 before singing. Choose a tempo and span that allow an easy short phrase, or shorten the voiced part and label your exact adapted task.
messages.3a07e98e6bc528fb: Original contour in quarter-note beats. M = your comfortable centre; L/H = nearby lower/higher, not quieter/louder. Each letter starts a new sound. R = counted silence. No fixed note or interval.
messages.a754540dab413bd4: A semitone is the nearest key to the right or left, black or white. A sharp ♯ raises a note by one semitone: F♯ is the black key right of F. A flat ♭ lowers it: B♭ is the black key left of B. One black key has two names, so F♯ and G♭ share a key. A natural ♮ cancels a sharp or flat. E–F and B–C are semitones with no black key between them.
messages.86ceb2d75dba4c7a: With right finger 2, touch C4 then each next semitone up to C5, naming each key aloud with a sharp name. Return down naming flats. Then play F4 F♯4 G4 and B4 B♭4 A4 slowly with relaxed fingers. A sign lasts until the end of its bar unless a natural cancels it.
messages.5ed7b20c3f870697: Can I name both possible names of a black key and find E–F and B–C?
messages.65dd6df344fd7bde: If names mix up, go back to lesson 2 and find the two-black-key groups first; then move one semitone at a time and say the direction before the name.
messages.cdf0e3b946b8249b: Intervals from a second to a fifth
messages.3863f3d4ccbd12e6: An interval counts letter names from one note to another, including both. C to D is a second (line to space), C to E a third (line to line or space to space), C to F a fourth, C to G a fifth. On the staff a second moves to the next position; a third skips one position; a fifth skips three. In a five-finger position the finger difference plus one gives the interval.
messages.776bca9c83f16de0: In right-hand C position play C4–D4, C4–E4, C4–F4, C4–G4, naming each interval before playing. Then read these pairs from the staff in your head first: E4–G4, D4–G4, F4–G4, C4–F4. Name, play, and compare only afterwards. Repeat with left hand C3–G3.
messages.708d23bb9cb91747: Can I name an interval from the staff before I play it?
messages.3525b5176c08b942: If counting slips, count letter names on your fingers including the first note, then check line/space pattern; a third always stays line–line or space–space.
messages.9e85464c23d40c92: G position and moving the hand
messages.4ab43466293ab742: A five-finger position is named by the lowest note it covers. In right-hand G position, fingers 1–5 cover G4 A4 B4 C5 D5. In left-hand G position, fingers 5–1 cover G2 A2 B2 C3 D3. Moving position means lifting the whole hand during a rest or a held note, not stretching one finger. G major uses F♯; when a melody meets F, play the black key F♯ unless a natural is written.
messages.9f905221bfd1ab14: Right hand: play C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 in C position, rest one beat while moving finger 1 to G4, then play G4 A4 B4 C5 D5. Then play this G-position phrase: G4 A4 B4 G4 | A4 F♯4 G4 half. F♯ is reached with finger 1 moving one key left of G or with a short shift; choose the comfortable option and keep the shoulder low.
messages.f35c11b312bcb56f: Can I move to a new position during a rest without rushing the count?
messages.21fd7214f6a4f236: If the move is late, practise only the last note, the rest and the first note of the new position, counting aloud; place the hand silently before playing.
messages.59237ad37ed88220: C major scale with a thumb crossing
messages.b6cf3e3e399d6168: A scale is a stepwise order of notes. C major uses only white keys: C D E F G A B C. One octave in the right hand is fingered 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5: after finger 3 plays E, the thumb passes under to F. Descending, finger 3 crosses over the thumb from F to E. The left hand ascends 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1: finger 3 crosses over to A. Keep the wrist level and let the arm travel.
messages.fe720e863354f060: First practise only the crossing: right E4 (3) to F4 (1) and back, slowly ten times with a release between. Then play C4 to C5 and back, one note per beat at a slow tempo. Left hand alone: C3 to C4 and back with 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1. Hands together only if each hand is even.
messages.de4bb27f570f9bd8: Is the crossing note as even in time as its neighbours?
messages.535751df7e784310: If the thumb bumps or the elbow lifts, slow down and play only three notes around the crossing; let the elbow move sideways with the hand.
messages.805e1f1d379f4d4a: In 3/4 each bar has three quarter-note beats, counted 1 2 3, with beat 1 slightly stronger. A dot adds half of a note's value: a dotted half lasts three beats, a dotted quarter lasts one and a half. A dotted quarter is often followed by an eighth: count 1 (2) and | the eighth falls on the 'and' of beat 2.
messages.8d69e8924b2c429a: Clap and count before playing. 3/4: C4 E4 G4 | C5 dotted half | G4 E4 C4 | dotted half C4. 4/4 with dotted rhythm: C4 dotted quarter, D4 eighth, E4 half | E4 dotted quarter, D4 eighth, C4 half. Then play each line with the right hand in C position, counting aloud.
messages.10c933c82dac1fd9: Does each bar add up to its time signature without an extra or missing beat?
messages.35d3a3b7f0cc030c: If the dotted rhythm becomes even, count in eighths (1 and 2 and) and hold the dotted note through three of them before the short note.
messages.9ec374ca939d23ae: Legato connects notes: release one key exactly as the next sounds. Staccato, a dot above or below the notehead, means short and detached; the key rises quickly but the beat keeps its full length. An accent > asks for one note a little stronger than its neighbours. These are touch choices, not force; keep the hand loose.
messages.71943ef7f39a6c08: Play C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 three ways at the same slow tempo: all legato, all staccato, then legato with an accent on each beat 1. Then play G4 F4 E4 D4 C4 with the first two staccato and the last three legato. Listen for silence between staccato notes while the count continues.
messages.93b7ec2ee4592433: Can I keep the same tempo while changing only the touch?
messages.6cd83c66f224a002: If staccato speeds you up, tap the pulse with the other hand or foot and play staccato only on every other beat first.
messages.160358f6a645d612: Left-hand C, F and G7 chords
messages.d1141237f38f676a: In C major the main chords are I (C), IV (F) and V7 (G7). A close left-hand pattern avoids big jumps: C chord C3 E3 G3 with fingers 5 3 1; F chord C3 F3 A3 with 5 2 1; G7 chord B2 F3 G3 with 5 2 1. C stays as a shared note between C and F; G stays between C and G7. Shared notes let the hand change with small finger moves.
messages.1f50f76c99ce8b60: Left hand alone, one chord per bar as a whole note: C | F | C | G7 | C. Move only the fingers that change. Then accompany this original right-hand melody in C position: E4 G4 E4 C4 | D4 F4 D4 G4 | F4 E4 D4 half | C4 whole, with left chords C | G7 | G7 | C held for each bar.
messages.0c1a29254dedde0c: Can I change chords on beat 1 while the melody keeps its rhythm?
messages.ea116dc6ee05593d: If the change is late, play only the last melody note and the new chord together several times; then add one bar before it.
messages.490614841162cad1: Map a new piece on your own
messages.8d261103d932a69e: Independent practice starts before playing. Choose a short beginner piece you are allowed to use, or write your own eight bars in C or G. Map it on paper: key and sharps/flats, time signature, the hand positions and where they move, the hardest two bars, and any dynamics or touch marks. A map turns a page into small, ordered tasks.
messages.43cc72bd172837f5: Write your map in five lines. Then choose the order: the hardest bars first, hands separately, slowly; then connect bars in pairs. Set a starting tempo you can keep without stopping. Do not look for a recording of the piece as a requirement; reading and counting are the goal here.
messages.1c9310a2f4830c55: Could someone else follow my map to know what to practise first?
messages.dcff1d74c6a56442: If the piece feels too hard, choose fewer bars or a piece in one position; a smaller complete map is better than a long unfinished one.
messages.e16983bda4075814: A practice cycle has four parts: a short warm-up (lesson 19 scale or lesson 17 intervals), focused work on one mapped problem, a full play-through at the chosen tempo, and a note for next time. Short regular sessions usually help more than one long session. Rest when hands or shoulders feel tense.
messages.4f1638d7333b40e0: On one day run the cycle with your lesson 23 piece: warm-up, one focus task, one play-through, one written note (bar, count, observed result). On another day repeat the same play-through at the same tempo and compare that bar: improved, unchanged or uncertain. Then write the next focus and, only if comfortable, a slightly faster tempo.
messages.e065f82a12230967: Can I plan, run and compare a practice session without the course telling me each step?
messages.b60097bd280717ba: If a session goes badly, shorten it to the warm-up and one bar; a finished small cycle still counts. A teacher can help with individual technique.
messages.c92f6f6432039d7d: Review key direction and C locations, finger numbers, both clef anchors and durations, sharps and flats, intervals, G position, the C major scale, 3/4 and dotted rhythms, touch marks and the left-hand C, F and G7 chords. Perform lesson 15, decode lesson 14 afresh and run one cycle with your own mapped piece from lessons 23–24. Your own observation is not a sensor result or mastery certificate. This is a bounded beginner foundation, not grade equivalence or complete piano training.
messages.be9753e94bc7af47: On separate days, try naming/reading, steady counting, the two-hand study and your own piece. Revisit the matching lesson when uncertain. A device-limited dynamics check stays unassessed (13). A teacher can help with individual technique and notation.

messages.8991b3e5a178cc23: Five small steps up and down
messages.0f655763bb42b5ed: Extend the L/M/H idea into a short stair: number five small, even-feeling steps 1 2 3 4 5, starting from a comfortable low tone near your L. Each step only moves a little higher than the one before. This is a personal relative pattern; exact interval sizes, a key or a note name are not checked. Keep volume the same on every step.
messages.032ef6620567271d: Hum 1 2 3 2 1 slowly, one quarter count each, then rest a bar. If comfortable, hum 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2 1. Write which step felt least easy, or “uncertain”. If the top step strains, stop at 3 and keep that smaller stair.
messages.761dcf140515f81b: Can I go up and back down by small steps without getting louder at the top?
messages.1cd74350a528ac72: If steps blur, speak the numbers on one tone first, then hum only 1 2 1 and 2 3 2; a smaller stair is a valid choice.
messages.d92355c3260e7411: A skip leaves out a step: 1 3 means moving from step 1 to step 3 without singing 2. Returning to 1 after a skip helps you check that your home tone stayed the same. Think the missing step silently if it helps. Accuracy is not measured here; you compare by your own listening.
messages.3270b663e016e316: Hum 1 2 3 then 1 3, with a rest between. Then try 1 3 1 and 3 5 3 if your five-step stair was comfortable. Read this contour silently first, then hum it: 1 3 2 1 | 3 5 3 R. Each number is one quarter count; R is a counted silence.
messages.acdab0331d9759e9: After a skip, does my return to 1 feel like the same home tone?
messages.754b48448a7cea71: If the skip lands unclear, sing the full steps 1 2 3, then repeat 1 3 while thinking 2; record “uncertain” rather than guessing.
messages.5128c50eda0774c7: A crescendo < grows gradually louder; a diminuendo > fades gradually softer. Volume and pitch are separate: a crescendo on one tone stays on the same tone. Stay inside a comfortable range of loudness; louder never means pushing the throat. Breath support for a phrase comes from an easy inhale, not a forced one.
messages.4b843f9b3b1c49f4: On a comfortable hum of M, count four beats: grow a little on 1–2, fade on 3–4, then rest a bar. Then speak “one two three four” with the same shape. Finally hum the 1 2 3 2 1 stair with a gentle crescendo up and diminuendo down, keeping the top step no louder than easy speech.
messages.185d76f4f69bc6d6: Can I change loudness gradually while the tone stays easy?
messages.53c09000bc03d5d9: If the throat tightens, return to speaking volume and practise only the fade; a smaller range of loudness is fine.
messages.59bd1f06d46ddaa8: Your own warm-up and stop signals
messages.889666cf65b14974: A warm-up prepares, it does not test. Build a short order from earlier lessons: settle and breathe (2–3), a gentle hum (4), short starts and releases (5), a small stair (16). Keep it about five minutes. Stop signals: pain, hoarseness that lasts, a scratchy throat, breathlessness or dizziness. Then rest; lasting voice problems need a qualified professional. This course gives no medical advice.
messages.ca31d1a7355c28a4: Write your warm-up as four lines with a time for each. Try it once today. Afterwards write one word for how the voice felt (easy / effortful / uncertain) and one change for next time. Water and short breaks are allowed at any point.
messages.ae04bb7e06d890b4: Do I know my warm-up order and when I must stop?
messages.19411f0439194991: If a warm-up step feels effortful, remove it and keep the breath and hum only; a shorter warm-up is still a warm-up.
messages.43e5a07f899ecf51: Map a short melody you choose
messages.dfd4878b9476a695: Choose a short melody you already know and may sing for yourself, such as a traditional children's tune, or write your own four bars with the contour symbols. Do not copy song lyrics into notes you share. Map it: where phrases end, where you will breathe, which part goes highest, and a relative contour using L M H or steps 1–5. A map makes the melody practisable in small parts.
messages.311416906795ecce: Write the map in four lines: phrases, breath marks, highest part, contour. Speak the words or a neutral syllable in rhythm first. Then hum one phrase at a time, resting between phrases. If the highest part strains, choose a lower starting tone or keep that phrase spoken.
messages.e0caaf76b57f00b6: Can I show where each phrase breathes and where the melody goes highest?
messages.8717ec23793163b4: If the melody is too long, map only its first phrase; a short complete map is better than a long guess.
messages.561b9522aad27503: An independent session has four parts: your warm-up (19), one focus from your map (20), one comfortable run of the melody, and a written note. Short, regular sessions usually help more than long ones. Comfort decides the length; stopping is always a valid result.

messages.00505c2ab9c65cc3: Written in 4→1 string order, G is 0232: index 1 on string 3 fret 2, middle 2 on string 1 fret 2, ring 3 on string 2 fret 3; string 4 open. Em is 0432: ring 3 on string 3 fret 4, middle 2 on string 2 fret 3, index 1 on string 1 fret 2. G and Em share the notes G and B. A comfortable alternative Em is 0402 if the full shape is too wide.
messages.1a29082eeeeb83ac: Form G, pluck each string separately, then strum gently four downstrokes. Do the same for Em. Then change G | Em | G | Em, one bar each, strumming on beat 1 and letting it ring, forming the next chord during beat 4.
messages.89bacf166cc822f3: Does every string of G and Em sound clearly before I add rhythm?
messages.4c8adfd90d26884d: If a string is muted, pluck strings one at a time and adjust the finger touching it; arch the finger and place it just behind the fret wire.
messages.6872393d89e88dce: Dm is 2210: middle 2 on string 4 fret 2, ring 3 on string 3 fret 2, index 1 on string 2 fret 1; string 1 open. A7 is 0100: index 1 on string 3 fret 1, other strings open. In the key of F, F, Dm and C belong together; A7 leads well into Dm. Notice that F (2010) and Dm (2210) differ by one finger.
messages.bcd70f421cda3a53: Change F → Dm by adding one finger, back and forth slowly. Then play A7 → Dm. Then the loop F | Dm | A7 | Dm, one bar each with four downstrokes, keeping fingers that stay in place on the strings.
messages.4e073202db4f5487: Can I keep the shared finger down when changing F to Dm?
messages.26814232676a1a46: If Dm buzzes, check that the index on fret 1 is close to the fret wire and the ring finger does not touch string 2.
messages.de19d769e57c1f2d: A common strum and a waltz strum
messages.df507592eb043c6d: A strum pattern places D and U in the eight half-beat slots of a bar. A common pattern is D, D U, U D U: slots D · D U · U D U, with no stroke on the 'and' of 1 and on beat 3. Keep the hand moving down and up all the time; only touch the strings where a stroke is written. In 3/4 a simple waltz strum is D D D or D D U D U.
messages.af944b6a9df595b7: On a muted strum (left hand resting lightly on the strings), count 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & and play D · D U · U D U for four bars. Then play it on C. Then on C | Am | F | G7. For 3/4, play D D U D U on C | G | G | C, counting 1 & 2 & 3 &.
messages.fa0b2980d7414d9e: Does my hand keep moving evenly even where there is no stroke?
messages.8d69bad37a0e819b: If the pattern falls apart, play only D on every beat, then add the U before beat 3 and 4, one addition at a time.
messages.3006aa2cd413895a: Fingerpicking plays chord notes one at a time. Let the thumb p play string 4 (and sometimes 3), index i string 2 and middle m string 1. A simple pattern over one bar of 4/4 in eighths: p i m i p i m i. Hold the full chord shape so each note rings into the next.
messages.9d482c06053a0875: Without the left hand, play open strings p i m i p i m i slowly for four bars. Then hold C and play the pattern for two bars, then Am for two bars. Then C | Am | F | G7 with one bar each. Keep the thumb relaxed and the wrist still.
messages.12f67b9990e15cf9: Are the eight notes even, and does the chord keep ringing?
messages.a5c519bd9f3c88b9: If fingers tangle, practise only p i p i, then add m; say the finger names aloud in time.
messages.1bff4c8805422c17: From a chord chart to a song form
messages.77d79eeb5833bbcc: A chord chart lists chords per bar, often in sections such as verse and chorus. Repeat signs or written repeats tell you to play a section again. A short introduction (for example two bars of the first chord) and a clear ending (one strum on the last chord, let ring) make a performance feel complete.
messages.49b7deb87a05d4f3: Play this original chart with the lesson 20 strum: Intro C | C. Verse C | Am | F | G7 (twice). Chorus F | G7 | C | Am | F | G7 | C | C. End: one strum on C and let it ring. Count one silent bar before starting.
messages.e81f6cce3bcf6a77: Can I play through the sections without stopping at the joins?
messages.b3f7cf857e795d5a: If a join stops you, loop only the last bar of one section and the first bar of the next.
messages.2792f780434aa5fa: Map a chart and run your own practice cycle
messages.a61e6687c45c2aa6: Choose a chord chart you may use for yourself, or write your own with chords from this course. messages.d1204d747c9b5ad5: Write the map, then run one cycle and note: tempo, the hardest change and what you observed (late / muted string / lost strum / no observed issue / uncertain). On another day repeat the same play-through at the same tempo and compare that change: improved, unchanged or uncertain. Write the next focus.
messages.d48f386498d8913e: Can I plan, run and compare a practice session without step-by-step help?

messages.6a5cc792bb808541: Natural notes in the first five frets
messages.479260283acc5f60: Natural notes are the letter names without sharps or flats. In sounding pitch, frets 0–5: string 4 E1 F1 (1) G1 (3) A1 (5); string 3 A1 B1 (2) C2 (3) D2 (5); string 2 D2 E2 (2) F2 (3) G2 (5); string 1 G2 A2 (2) B2 (4) C3 (5). Fret 5 on one string sounds the same as the next higher open string, for example string 4 fret 5 A1 = open string 3.
messages.905771132200fe40: Say and play the natural notes on string 4 from E1 to A1, then on string 3 from A1 to D2, one note per beat. Then find A1 in two places (string 4 fret 5 and open string 3) and D2 in two places, and compare that they sound the same. Keep index on fret 1–2 and ring/little finger on fret 4–5 as comfortable.
messages.97134f661677a4c5: Can I name any natural note in frets 0–5 and find one note in two places?
messages.7d125b50d7e52a10: If you lose track, recite the letters E F G A B C D on string 4 aloud while pointing, then play only the notes on frets 0, 3 and 5.
messages.7726337998015ba0: A major scale has the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. On bass a movable one-octave shape starting with finger 2 on the root covers three strings: root (2), 2nd (4), 3rd next string (1), 4th (2), 5th (4), 6th next string (1), 7th (3), octave (4). From C2 at string 3 fret 3 this gives C2 D2 E2 F2 G2 A2 B2 C3.
messages.872372d7fe2d68c1: Play the C major shape up and down: string 3 frets 3 5; string 2 frets 2 3 5; string 1 frets 2 4 5. One note per beat, alternating i and m, at a slow tempo. Then move the same shape so the root is G1 on string 4 fret 3 and play it again.
messages.76172bd35fabac7c: Can I play the shape evenly and say the scale degree of each note?
messages.f6f7c9f8cab96433: If the stretch from fret 2 to 5 is uncomfortable, shift the hand by one fret for the top notes instead of reaching; comfort comes before the textbook fingering.
messages.c4f3951be11252e3: Approach notes into a chord change
messages.cfb9dce10eab18ec: An approach note on the last beat of a bar leads into the next root. A chromatic approach is one fret below or above the target root; a scale approach is the scale note next to it. For C to F, play E2 (one fret below F2) on beat 4; for F to G, play F♯2 or A2. The approach is short and leads, it does not replace the root on beat 1.
messages.f01acba67d5f7938: Imagine the chart C | F | G | C. Play roots on beats 1–3 and an approach on beat 4: C2 C2 C2 E2 | F2 F2 F2 F♯2 | G2 G2 G2 B1 | C2 whole. Use string 3 fret 3 for C2, string 3 fret 2 for B1 and string 2 for F2 and G2. Count aloud; then try your own approach choices.
messages.3fafc981193b4a55: Does each approach lead clearly into the next root on beat 1?
messages.c0259cf960ef0dc1: If the change arrives late, play only beat 4 and the next beat 1 several times, keeping the left hand moving during beat 4.
messages.a2749d007119f1d9: A twelve-bar blues in A uses A7, D7 and E7 in the order A A A A | D D A A | E D A E. A common bass line plays root, third, fifth, sixth: over A that is A1 C♯2 E2 F♯2; over D it is D2 F♯2 A2 B2; over E it is E1 G♯1 B1 C♯2. Play them as quarter notes, one pattern per bar.
messages.0933ad266ff77ab2: Learn the A pattern first: open string 3, string 3 fret 4, string 2 fret 2, string 2 fret 4. Move it to D (open string 2, string 2 fret 4, string 1 fret 2, string 1 fret 4) and to E (open string 4, string 4 fret 4, string 3 fret 2, string 3 fret 4). Then play all twelve bars at a slow tempo with a counted bar before starting.
messages.343bd05539c32840: Can I keep track of where I am in the twelve bars without stopping?
messages.e72f94ca0779fd77: If you get lost, say the chord name on beat 1 of each bar while playing only roots, then add the pattern back one line of four bars at a time.
messages.6453f24eb93b5f55: Play with an external pulse and control note length
messages.5088744c7045ec18: A bassist keeps time for others. Use any external metronome or drum loop you already have; this course does not supply sound. Start slow enough that every note lands with the click. Note length is part of the groove: legato notes ring until the next one, staccato notes stop early with a gentle left-hand release or right-hand touch while the beat continues.
messages.c2bd8d1ba814fae4: Set a slow click. Play the lesson 21 blues roots as quarter notes, all legato for four bars, then all staccato for four bars. Then play half notes, ending each exactly on the next beat. Note your tempo and whether notes landed with the click: on time / early / late / uncertain.
messages.e45cdb6f1f3bfe27: Can I keep the click and choose short or long notes on purpose?
messages.3d8deb0b8630b2a8: If you drift from the click, play only on beat 1 of each bar and count the other beats silently, then add beats back.
